summary:
MISSION FORGE: HYDROGUARD is an experimental adaptive observation-planning system. It uses NASA POWER precipitation and temperature data to identify changing environmental conditions and prioritize proposed follow-up observations. Its purpose is to demonstrate how future Earth-observation missions could allocate limited observation resources more intelligently.

Users can design a spacecraft, select scientific instruments, configure mission systems, and evaluate simplified engineering constraints such as mass, power, communications, and budget. The integrated HydroGuard Earth Data Lab retrieves NASA POWER daily precipitation and temperature data for selected study locations. It compares recent 30-day periods and uses a transparent experimental scoring method to prioritize proposed follow-up observations.

The project's proposed innovation is an adaptive observation architecture that directs limited observation resources toward locations showing stronger environmental changes. HYDROGUARD demonstrates how space technology, open Earth data, and interactive mission planning could support better water-management decisions. It is an educational prototype, not an operational drought-warning system.
details:
What HYDROGUARD does

HYDROGUARD combines an interactive spacecraft-design simulator with an experimental Earth-observation data application.

The project has three main components:

1. Mission Forge Simulator

Users configure a proposed spacecraft by selecting scientific instruments, spacecraft subsystems, power systems, communications, propulsion, orbit, launch class, mission duration, and budget. The simulator evaluates simplified engineering constraints, including spacecraft mass, available power, data capacity, and estimated cost.

2. NASA Earth Data Lab

The application connects to the NASA POWER Daily API and requests daily precipitation and 2-meter air-temperature data for four sample study locations: Kathmandu, Dhaka, Nairobi, and Phoenix. It compares two adjacent 30-day periods to identify changes in rainfall and temperature.

3. Adaptive Observation Scheduler

A transparent experimental scoring method converts observed changes into a proposed allocation of 100 observation credits. These credits prioritize precipitation mapping, thermal observation, and proposed soil-moisture confirmation.

Innovationcan

The proposed innovation is an adaptive Earth-observation architecture. Rather than assigning equal observation priority to every location, the concept reallocates limited observation opportunities toward regions showing stronger environmental changes.

The longer-term concept includes a cooperative satellite constellation, targeted revisit requests, and an information layer for environmental researchers and water-management organizations.

Intended Impact

The project explores how satellite observations could complement local environmental measurements and support better-informed water-management and agricultural planning.

Technology Used

  • HTML5 for application structure
  • CSS3 for responsive interface and visual design
  • JavaScript for mission calculations, simulator interactions, data processing, and API integration
  • NASA POWER Daily API for precipitation and temperature data
  • Browser Fetch API for retrieving NASA data

No physical satellite hardware was built. All spacecraft engineering values are illustrative educational parameters.

Limitations and Future Development

The experimental score is not an official drought index, validated forecast, or public warning. NASA POWER estimates are not substitutes for local rain-gauge measurements. Soil moisture is a proposed follow-up observation and is not directly measured in the current data request.

Future development could integrate NASA SMAP soil-moisture and GPM precipitation observations, validate the scoring method against established drought indicators, and develop a more detailed orbital and engineering model.
